title: Pharmacological Biochemistry & Toxicology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Pharmacological Biochemistry & Toxicology curriculum: xenobiotic biotransformation (Phase I/II reactions), cytochrome P450 pharmacology, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics fundamentals, mechanisms of chemical toxicity and organ-specific toxicology, heavy metal and pesticide toxicology, and detoxification/antidote biochemistry.

questions.question: Phase I biotransformation reactions of xenobiotics are primarily characterized by which of the following?
options: Introduction or exposure of a functional group (e.g. -OH, -NH2, -COOH) via oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis
Conjugation of the xenobiotic with an endogenous polar molecule such as glucuronic acid
Irreversible covalent binding of the xenobiotic to plasma proteins
Active transport of the xenobiotic across the intestinal brush border
questions.correct_answer: Introduction or exposure of a functional group (e.g. -OH, -NH2, -COOH) via oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Phase I reactions chemically modify a xenobiotic by oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis to introduce or unmask a reactive functional group, which often increases polarity slightly and creates a handle for Phase II conjugation.

questions.question: Which enzyme system is chiefly responsible for the majority of Phase I oxidative drug metabolism in the liver?
options: Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases
Glutathione S-transferases
UDP-glucuronosyltransferases
Sulfotransferases
questions.correct_answer: Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases
questions.explanation: The cytochrome P450 (CYP) superfamily, located mainly in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes, catalyzes the majority of oxidative Phase I reactions on lipophilic xenobiotics.

questions.question: Glucuronidation, a major Phase II conjugation reaction, involves the transfer of glucuronic acid from which activated donor molecule?
options: UDP-glucuronic acid
Acetyl-CoA
PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate)
S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)
questions.correct_answer: UDP-glucuronic acid
questions.explanation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs) transfer glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid to a nucleophilic group on the substrate, forming a water-soluble glucuronide that is readily excreted.

questions.question: Sulfation of xenobiotics (Phase II) uses which compound as the sulfate donor?
options: PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate)
UDP-glucuronic acid
Glutathione
Acetyl-CoA
questions.correct_answer: PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate)
questions.explanation: Sulfotransferases catalyze transfer of a sulfate group from the universal sulfate donor PAPS to hydroxyl or amine groups on xenobiotics, typically producing a highly water-soluble sulfate ester.

questions.question: Acetylation of xenobiotics such as isoniazid is catalyzed by which class of enzyme, and shows what well-known form of genetic variation in humans?
options: N-acetyltransferases (NAT), which show fast- and slow-acetylator polymorphisms
Glutathione S-transferases, which show no genetic variation
UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, which are absent in humans
Cytochrome P450 2D6, which is only expressed in the kidney
questions.correct_answer: N-acetyltransferases (NAT), which show fast- and slow-acetylator polymorphisms
questions.explanation: N-acetyltransferase (particularly NAT2) activity is genetically polymorphic, and 'slow acetylators' metabolize drugs like isoniazid more slowly, predisposing them to higher drug accumulation and toxicity.

questions.question: The 'first-pass effect' in pharmacokinetics refers to which phenomenon?
options: Extensive hepatic metabolism of an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation, reducing its bioavailability
The initial rapid distribution of a drug into highly perfused tissues
The first dose of a drug producing an exaggerated therapeutic effect
Renal filtration of a drug immediately after intravenous injection
questions.correct_answer: Extensive hepatic metabolism of an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation, reducing its bioavailability
questions.explanation: Orally administered drugs are absorbed into the portal circulation and pass through the liver before reaching systemic circulation; extensive hepatic metabolism at this stage can substantially reduce the fraction of active drug that becomes systemically available.

questions.question: Bioavailability (F) of a drug is best defined as:
options: The fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation in an unchanged, active form
The total amount of drug bound to plasma proteins
The rate at which a drug is eliminated from the body
The volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time
questions.correct_answer: The fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation in an unchanged, active form
questions.explanation: Bioavailability quantifies how much of an administered dose actually reaches the systemic circulation intact; an intravenous dose has a bioavailability of 100%, against which other routes are compared.

questions.question: A drug has an apparent volume of distribution (Vd) far exceeding total body water (e.g. several hundred litres in a 70 kg adult). This most likely indicates that the drug is:
options: Extensively sequestered in tissues outside the plasma compartment (e.g. bound to tissue proteins or lipid)
Confined entirely to the plasma compartment
Rapidly and completely excreted unchanged in urine
Unable to cross the capillary endothelium
questions.correct_answer: Extensively sequestered in tissues outside the plasma compartment (e.g. bound to tissue proteins or lipid)
questions.explanation: A very large apparent Vd implies that most of the drug resides outside the plasma in tissues rather than remaining in the blood, so the plasma concentration is much lower than would be predicted from the dose alone.

questions.question: In first-order elimination kinetics, which statement correctly describes the relationship between drug concentration and rate of elimination?
options: The rate of elimination is proportional to the plasma drug concentration, and a constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time
A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time regardless of concentration
Elimination rate is independent of drug concentration once metabolic enzymes are saturated
The half-life increases as the dose increases
questions.correct_answer: The rate of elimination is proportional to the plasma drug concentration, and a constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time
questions.explanation: Most drugs follow first-order kinetics, where elimination rate is proportional to concentration; this produces a constant half-life that is independent of the dose administered.

questions.question: Zero-order elimination kinetics, as seen with ethanol at typical consumption levels, is characterized by which feature?
options: A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time because the metabolizing enzyme system is saturated
Elimination rate is proportional to plasma concentration
Half-life remains constant regardless of dose
The drug is eliminated entirely by renal filtration without metabolism
questions.correct_answer: A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time because the metabolizing enzyme system is saturated
questions.explanation: When the enzyme(s) responsible for elimination become saturated, the elimination rate plateaus at a fixed amount per unit time regardless of concentration, so the concept of a fixed half-life no longer strictly applies.

questions.question: A drug is given as a rapid IV bolus of 500 mg, and the resulting initial plasma concentration is 10 mg/L. What is the apparent volume of distribution (Vd)?
options: 5 L
questions.explanation: Vd = Dose / C0 = 500 mg / 10 mg/L = 50 L, since Vd relates the administered dose to the resulting initial plasma concentration.

questions.question: A drug has a plasma half-life of 4 hours. Approximately what fraction of the drug remains in the body after 12 hours (three half-lives), assuming first-order kinetics and no further dosing?
questions.explanation: After each half-life the remaining fraction halves: 100% to 50% to 25% to 12.5% after three half-lives (12 hours), consistent with first-order elimination.

questions.question: The therapeutic index (TI) of a drug is defined as the ratio of which two parameters, and what does a low TI imply clinically?
options: TD50 (or LD50) to ED50; a low TI means a narrow margin between effective and toxic doses, requiring careful dose monitoring
ED50 to TD50; a low TI means the drug is very safe
Vd to clearance; a low TI means rapid elimination
Bioavailability to clearance; a low TI means poor absorption
questions.correct_answer: TD50 (or LD50) to ED50; a low TI means a narrow margin between effective and toxic doses, requiring careful dose monitoring
questions.explanation: The therapeutic index compares the dose producing toxicity in 50% of subjects to the dose producing the desired effect in 50%; a low ratio indicates a narrow safety margin, as seen with drugs like warfarin or digoxin.

questions.question: A partial agonist acting at the same receptor as a full agonist, when given alone, will produce:
options: A submaximal response even at full receptor occupancy, because it has lower intrinsic efficacy than a full agonist
The same maximal response as the full agonist
No response at all, behaving purely as an antagonist
An effect only when co-administered with the full agonist
questions.correct_answer: A submaximal response even at full receptor occupancy, because it has lower intrinsic efficacy than a full agonist
questions.explanation: A partial agonist has affinity for the receptor but lower intrinsic efficacy than a full agonist, so it cannot produce the maximal system response even when all receptors are occupied.

questions.question: Competitive antagonism at a receptor is characterized pharmacologically by which effect on the agonist dose-response curve?
options: A parallel rightward shift of the curve with an unchanged maximal response, which can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration
A downward shift in maximal response that cannot be overcome by increasing agonist concentration
No change in the curve at all
A leftward shift indicating increased agonist potency
questions.correct_answer: A parallel rightward shift of the curve with an unchanged maximal response, which can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration
questions.explanation: A competitive antagonist reversibly competes with the agonist for the same binding site, so increasing agonist concentration can outcompete the antagonist and still achieve the full maximal effect, shifting the curve rightward without lowering the ceiling.

questions.question: Rifampicin is a classic example of a cytochrome P450 enzyme inducer. What is the clinical consequence of co-administering rifampicin with another drug metabolized by the induced CYP isoenzyme?
options: Accelerated metabolism of the co-administered drug, potentially reducing its plasma concentration and therapeutic effect
Inhibited metabolism of the co-administered drug, leading to toxic accumulation
No effect, since rifampicin is not metabolized by CYP enzymes
Complete blockade of the co-administered drug's absorption
questions.correct_answer: Accelerated metabolism of the co-administered drug, potentially reducing its plasma concentration and therapeutic effect
questions.explanation: Rifampicin upregulates expression of several CYP450 isoenzymes (notably CYP3A4), increasing the metabolic clearance of co-administered drugs and potentially causing therapeutic failure, as is a known concern with oral contraceptives and some antiretrovirals.

questions.question: Cimetidine is well known clinically for which pharmacokinetic interaction property?
options: It inhibits several cytochrome P450 isoenzymes, slowing the metabolism and increasing plasma levels of co-administered drugs
It strongly induces cytochrome P450 enzymes, accelerating drug metabolism
It has no effect on hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes
It selectively enhances Phase II glucuronidation only
questions.correct_answer: It inhibits several cytochrome P450 isoenzymes, slowing the metabolism and increasing plasma levels of co-administered drugs
questions.explanation: Cimetidine binds to and inhibits multiple CYP450 isoenzymes, reducing the metabolic clearance of many co-administered drugs (e.g. warfarin, phenytoin) and raising the risk of toxicity.

questions.question: Furanocoumarins present in grapefruit juice cause clinically significant drug interactions primarily through which mechanism?
options: Irreversible inhibition of intestinal CYP3A4, increasing the oral bioavailability of susceptible drugs
Induction of hepatic CYP450 enzymes, decreasing drug bioavailability
Chelation of the drug in the gut lumen, preventing absorption entirely
Direct displacement of the drug from plasma protein binding sites
questions.correct_answer: Irreversible inhibition of intestinal CYP3A4, increasing the oral bioavailability of susceptible drugs
questions.explanation: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit juice mechanism-based (irreversibly) inhibit CYP3A4 in the intestinal wall, reducing first-pass metabolism and thereby increasing the systemic exposure of drugs such as certain statins and calcium channel blockers.

questions.question: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) hepatotoxicity at overdose is mechanistically explained by which sequence of events?
options: Glucuronidation/sulfation pathways become saturated, shunting more paracetamol through CYP450 to form the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which depletes hepatic glutathione and covalently binds hepatocyte macromolecules
Paracetamol directly inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase in hepatocytes
Paracetamol is excreted unchanged and causes toxicity via renal crystal formation
Paracetamol induces excessive glucuronidation, which itself is directly hepatotoxic
questions.correct_answer: Glucuronidation/sulfation pathways become saturated, shunting more paracetamol through CYP450 to form the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which depletes hepatic glutathione and covalently binds hepatocyte macromolecules
questions.explanation: At therapeutic doses most paracetamol is safely conjugated, but at overdose the normal Phase II pathways saturate, so a larger fraction is oxidized by CYP2E1/CYP3A4 to the reactive electrophile NAPQI; once glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocellular proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis.

questions.question: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is the standard antidote for paracetamol overdose. Its primary mechanism of action is:
options: Acting as a glutathione precursor/substitute to replenish hepatic glutathione stores and detoxify the reactive metabolite NAPQI
Directly inhibiting cytochrome P450 enzymes to block paracetamol metabolism entirely
Chelating the reactive metabolite to promote urinary excretion
Enhancing renal clearance of unmetabolized paracetamol
questions.correct_answer: Acting as a glutathione precursor/substitute to replenish hepatic glutathione stores and detoxify the reactive metabolite NAPQI
questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine supplies cysteine to replenish depleted intracellular glutathione (and can itself act as a glutathione substitute/precursor), allowing conjugation and detoxification of NAPQI before it causes further hepatocellular damage.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of glutathione S-transferase (GST) in Phase II detoxification?
options: It catalyzes conjugation of glutathione's cysteine thiol group with electrophilic xenobiotics or reactive metabolites, facilitating their excretion
It hydrolyzes ester bonds in xenobiotics
It oxidizes xenobiotics using molecular oxygen and NADPH
It methylates xenobiotics using S-adenosylmethionine
questions.correct_answer: It catalyzes conjugation of glutathione's cysteine thiol group with electrophilic xenobiotics or reactive metabolites, facilitating their excretion
questions.explanation: GST catalyzes nucleophilic attack of glutathione's thiol group on electrophilic centers of reactive intermediates, neutralizing their reactivity and forming conjugates that are further processed to mercapturic acids for excretion.

questions.question: Lipid peroxidation, a key mechanism of chemical-induced cell injury, primarily damages which cellular structure and by what process?
options: Cell membranes, via free-radical attack on polyunsaturated fatty acids, generating a self-propagating chain reaction that compromises membrane integrity
The nucleus, via direct hydrolysis of DNA phosphodiester bonds
The Golgi apparatus, via osmotic swelling
Ribosomes, via inhibition of peptidyl transferase activity
questions.correct_answer: Cell membranes, via free-radical attack on polyunsaturated fatty acids, generating a self-propagating chain reaction that compromises membrane integrity
questions.explanation: Reactive oxygen species abstract hydrogen atoms from polyunsaturated fatty acids in membrane phospholipids, initiating a self-propagating chain reaction of lipid peroxidation that disrupts membrane fluidity and integrity, ultimately contributing to cell death.

questions.question: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated during xenobiotic metabolism include which of the following?
options: Superoxide anion, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radical
Only molecular oxygen
Carbon dioxide and water exclusively
Nitrogen gas and ammonia
questions.correct_answer: Superoxide anion, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radical
questions.explanation: Redox cycling of certain xenobiotics and normal one-electron reduction of oxygen during metabolism generate superoxide anion, which can be converted to hydrogen peroxide and, via Fenton chemistry, to the highly reactive hydroxyl radical.

questions.question: Covalent binding of a reactive metabolite to cellular macromolecules (proteins, lipids, nucleic acids) is significant in toxicology chiefly because it can:
options: Alter or destroy the normal structure and function of the target macromolecule, potentially triggering cell injury, immune-mediated reactions, or mutagenesis
Always be rapidly and completely reversed by cellular repair enzymes with no consequence
Only occur with water-soluble, non-reactive metabolites
Have no bearing on carcinogenesis or hepatotoxicity
questions.correct_answer: Alter or destroy the normal structure and function of the target macromolecule, potentially triggering cell injury, immune-mediated reactions, or mutagenesis
questions.explanation: Covalent adduct formation can directly impair a protein's or nucleic acid's function, create neoantigens that provoke immune-mediated (idiosyncratic) drug reactions, or cause DNA mutations that initiate carcinogenesis.

questions.question: Benzo[a]pyrene, a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon found in tobacco smoke, requires metabolic activation to exert its carcinogenic effect. This activation proceeds mainly through:
options: CYP450-mediated epoxidation followed by epoxide hydrolase action to form a diol-epoxide that binds covalently to DNA
Direct binding of the parent compound to DNA without any metabolism
Renal excretion without any biotransformation
Simple Phase II glucuronidation that directly activates the compound
questions.correct_answer: CYP450-mediated epoxidation followed by epoxide hydrolase action to form a diol-epoxide that binds covalently to DNA
questions.explanation: Benzo[a]pyrene is a procarcinogen that is bioactivated by CYP450 enzymes and epoxide hydrolase to its ultimate carcinogenic form, benzo[a]pyrene-7,8-dihydrodiol-9,10-epoxide, which covalently binds guanine bases in DNA and can initiate mutagenesis.

questions.question: Aflatoxin B1, a mycotoxin produced by Aspergillus species, is bioactivated in the liver to a genotoxic epoxide that preferentially forms adducts with which DNA base, and is strongly associated with which cancer?
options: Guanine (forming AFB1-N7-guanine adducts), strongly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma
Thymine, associated with skin cancer
Cytosine, associated with lung cancer
Adenine, associated with colorectal cancer
questions.correct_answer: Guanine (forming AFB1-N7-guanine adducts), strongly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma
questions.explanation: CYP450 enzymes convert aflatoxin B1 to a reactive 8,9-epoxide that forms adducts predominantly at the N7 position of guanine in DNA, a mutagenic event strongly linked epidemiologically to hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly in regions with dietary aflatoxin exposure.

questions.question: The distinction between a 'genotoxic' and an 'epigenetic' (non-genotoxic) carcinogen lies in which feature?
options: A genotoxic carcinogen directly damages DNA (e.g. via adduct formation or mutation), whereas an epigenetic carcinogen promotes tumor development through mechanisms other than direct DNA damage, such as altered gene expression or sustained cell proliferation
A genotoxic carcinogen never requires metabolic activation, while an epigenetic carcinogen always does
Epigenetic carcinogens act only on RNA, never on proteins or DNA
There is no meaningful biochemical distinction between the two
questions.correct_answer: A genotoxic carcinogen directly damages DNA (e.g. via adduct formation or mutation), whereas an epigenetic carcinogen promotes tumor development through mechanisms other than direct DNA damage, such as altered gene expression or sustained cell proliferation
questions.explanation: Genotoxic carcinogens or their reactive metabolites interact directly with DNA to cause mutations, while epigenetic (non-genotoxic) carcinogens promote carcinogenesis through indirect mechanisms such as receptor-mediated altered gene expression, chronic cell proliferation, or immune suppression, without directly damaging DNA.

questions.question: Lead toxicity at the biochemical level classically inhibits which heme biosynthesis enzyme, producing a characteristic accumulation of its substrate?
options: Delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD), causing accumulation of delta-aminolevulinic acid
Ferrochelatase only, with no effect on any other enzyme
Heme oxygenase, causing accumulation of biliverdin
Succinate dehydrogenase, causing accumulation of succinate
questions.correct_answer: Delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD), causing accumulation of delta-aminolevulinic acid
questions.explanation: Lead has a high affinity for sulfhydryl groups and inhibits ALAD (and also ferrochelatase) in the heme biosynthetic pathway; ALAD inhibition is especially sensitive and leads to accumulation of delta-aminolevulinic acid, a useful biomarker of lead exposure.

questions.question: Mercury and other heavy metals such as arsenic and cadmium exert much of their cellular toxicity through which common biochemical mechanism?
options: High-affinity binding to sulfhydryl (-SH) groups on proteins and enzymes, disrupting their structure and catalytic function
Selective binding to carbohydrate hydroxyl groups only
Direct hydrolysis of peptide bonds in target proteins
Competitive inhibition of DNA polymerase exclusively
questions.correct_answer: High-affinity binding to sulfhydryl (-SH) groups on proteins and enzymes, disrupting their structure and catalytic function
questions.explanation: Heavy metals such as mercury, arsenic, and cadmium have strong chemical affinity for sulfhydryl groups found in cysteine residues of many enzymes and structural proteins, and binding to these groups disrupts protein conformation and enzymatic activity across many pathways.

questions.question: Arsenic (as arsenite, As3+) is particularly toxic to mitochondrial energy metabolism because it inhibits which enzyme complex by binding vicinal dithiol groups?
options: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (and other alpha-keto acid dehydrogenases requiring lipoic acid)
Hexokinase in the cytosol
DNA ligase in the nucleus
Carbonic anhydrase in erythrocytes
questions.correct_answer: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (and other alpha-keto acid dehydrogenases requiring lipoic acid)
questions.explanation: Arsenite binds the vicinal dithiol groups of lipoic acid, a cofactor required by pyruvate dehydrogenase and related alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes, thereby inhibiting the citric acid cycle's entry point and impairing cellular ATP production.

questions.question: Chelation therapy, used in the treatment of heavy metal poisoning, works on which biochemical principle?
options: A chelating agent forms a stable, water-soluble complex with the metal ion, facilitating its excretion and reducing free metal available to bind cellular targets
The chelator directly reverses the covalent binding of the metal to protein sulfhydryl groups
The chelator converts the metal ion into a gas that is exhaled
The chelator induces cytochrome P450 enzymes to metabolize the metal
questions.correct_answer: A chelating agent forms a stable, water-soluble complex with the metal ion, facilitating its excretion and reducing free metal available to bind cellular targets
questions.explanation: Chelating agents contain multiple donor atoms that coordinate the metal ion into a stable ring complex, lowering the concentration of free toxic metal and promoting its renal (or biliary) excretion.

questions.question: Cadmium accumulates chronically primarily in which organ, where it induces synthesis of a metal-binding protein as a protective (though ultimately limited) response?
options: The kidney, where it induces metallothionein synthesis
The lungs, where it induces surfactant protein synthesis
The pancreas, where it induces insulin synthesis
The skin, where it induces keratin synthesis
questions.correct_answer: The kidney, where it induces metallothionein synthesis
questions.explanation: Cadmium has a very long biological half-life and accumulates chiefly in the renal cortex, where it induces the cysteine-rich protein metallothionein to sequester the metal; however, chronic accumulation still eventually causes proximal tubular damage.

questions.question: Organophosphate pesticides (e.g. malathion, parathion) produce their toxic effects mainly through which biochemical mechanism?
options: Irreversible phosphorylation and inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine at synapses
Direct blockade of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors without affecting the enzyme that degrades acetylcholine
Inhibition of monoamine oxidase, causing accumulation of catecholamines
Direct inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase pump
questions.correct_answer: Irreversible phosphorylation and inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine at synapses
questions.explanation: Organophosphates covalently phosphorylate the serine hydroxyl group at the active site of acetylcholinesterase, inactivating the enzyme and leading to excessive accumulation of acetylcholine at cholinergic synapses, producing the classic cholinergic toxidrome.

questions.question: In organophosphate poisoning, atropine and pralidoxime are used together as antidotes. What is the distinct mechanism of each?
options: Atropine blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors to counter excess acetylcholine, while pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphate group from the enzyme
Both drugs work by directly destroying the organophosphate molecule in the bloodstream
Atropine reactivates acetylcholinesterase, while pralidoxime blocks muscarinic receptors
Both drugs act solely by inducing hepatic metabolism of the organophosphate
questions.correct_answer: Atropine blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors to counter excess acetylcholine, while pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphate group from the enzyme
questions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist that relieves the symptoms of excess acetylcholine, while pralidoxime is an oxime that can reactivate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase if given before the enzyme-phosphate bond 'ages' into an irreversible form.

questions.question: Why does 'aging' of the acetylcholinesterase-organophosphate complex render pralidoxime ineffective if treatment is delayed?
options: Aging involves loss of an alkyl group from the phosphorylated enzyme, converting the phosphate adduct to a form that is chemically resistant to oxime-induced reactivation
Aging refers to the natural degradation of pralidoxime itself over time
Aging means the organophosphate is completely metabolized and no longer bound to the enzyme
Aging increases the enzyme's affinity for pralidoxime, but the drug is no longer absorbed
questions.correct_answer: Aging involves loss of an alkyl group from the phosphorylated enzyme, converting the phosphate adduct to a form that is chemically resistant to oxime-induced reactivation
questions.explanation: Over time, the phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase can lose an alkyl group in a dealkylation reaction ('aging'), leaving a negatively charged phosphate adduct that oximes like pralidoxime can no longer displace, making early treatment critical.

questions.question: Ethanol is metabolized in the liver primarily by which enzyme in its first oxidative step, and what is the immediate product?
options: Alcohol dehydrogenase, producing acetaldehyde
Aldehyde dehydrogenase, producing acetate
Cytochrome P450 2E1 exclusively, producing acetic acid
Monoamine oxidase, producing formaldehyde
questions.correct_answer: Alcohol dehydrogenase, producing acetaldehyde
questions.explanation: Cytosolic alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde using NAD+ as a cofactor, generating NADH in the process; acetaldehyde is then further oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetate.
questions.topic: Alcohol and drugs of abuse biochemistry

questions.question: Chronic heavy alcohol consumption induces the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEOS), which involves which enzyme and contributes to which biochemical consequence?
options: CYP2E1, which is induced with chronic use and generates reactive oxygen species contributing to hepatocellular oxidative damage
Aldehyde dehydrogenase, which is induced and reduces oxidative stress
Alcohol dehydrogenase, which is completely replaced by MEOS at all consumption levels
Xanthine oxidase, which metabolizes ethanol directly to CO2 and water
questions.correct_answer: CYP2E1, which is induced with chronic use and generates reactive oxygen species contributing to hepatocellular oxidative damage
questions.explanation: Chronic ethanol exposure induces CYP2E1 as part of the MEOS pathway; this route generates reactive oxygen species as a byproduct, contributing to oxidative stress and hepatocellular injury on top of the effects of acetaldehyde accumulation.
questions.topic: Alcohol and drugs of abuse biochemistry

questions.question: Disulfiram, used in alcohol aversion therapy, produces unpleasant symptoms after alcohol ingestion by inhibiting which enzyme, leading to accumulation of which toxic intermediate?
options: Aldehyde dehydrogenase, leading to accumulation of acetaldehyde
Alcohol dehydrogenase, leading to accumulation of ethanol itself
Cytochrome P450 2E1, leading to accumulation of acetate
Monoamine oxidase, leading to accumulation of dopamine
questions.correct_answer: Aldehyde dehydrogenase, leading to accumulation of acetaldehyde
questions.explanation: Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde produced from ingested ethanol accumulates to toxic levels, causing the characteristic flushing, nausea, tachycardia, and hypotension of the disulfiram-ethanol reaction.
questions.topic: Alcohol and drugs of abuse biochemistry

questions.question: Chronic alcohol-induced NADH accumulation from ethanol oxidation contributes to which well-recognized metabolic disturbance?
options: Inhibition of gluconeogenesis and promotion of hepatic fatty acid synthesis, contributing to hypoglycemia and fatty liver
Enhanced gluconeogenesis leading to hyperglycemia
Decreased triglyceride synthesis and reduced fat accumulation in the liver
Increased beta-oxidation of fatty acids without any change in glucose metabolism
questions.correct_answer: Inhibition of gluconeogenesis and promotion of hepatic fatty acid synthesis, contributing to hypoglycemia and fatty liver
questions.explanation: The shift in the NADH/NAD+ ratio caused by ethanol oxidation inhibits gluconeogenic reactions requiring NAD+ and favors lipogenesis over fatty acid oxidation, contributing to alcoholic fatty liver and a risk of hypoglycemia, particularly after fasting.
questions.topic: Alcohol and drugs of abuse biochemistry

questions.question: Nephrotoxic injury from certain xenobiotics (e.g. aminoglycosides, heavy metals) preferentially targets which segment of the nephron, and why?
options: The proximal convoluted tubule, because it reabsorbs and concentrates filtered xenobiotics, exposing its cells to high intracellular concentrations
The glomerulus exclusively, because it has the highest blood flow
The distal convoluted tubule, because it has the lowest metabolic activity
The renal pelvis, because it stores urine before excretion
questions.correct_answer: The proximal convoluted tubule, because it reabsorbs and concentrates filtered xenobiotics, exposing its cells to high intracellular concentrations
questions.explanation: Proximal tubular cells actively reabsorb filtered solutes including many xenobiotics, concentrating them intracellularly to levels that can exceed those in plasma, which combined with high metabolic (mitochondrial) activity makes this segment especially vulnerable to toxic injury.

questions.question: Idiosyncratic drug reactions, which occur in a small subset of individuals independent of the normal dose-response relationship, are frequently attributed biochemically to which mechanism?
options: Formation of a reactive drug metabolite that binds host proteins to create a neoantigen, triggering an immune-mediated hypersensitivity response
A predictable, dose-dependent exaggeration of the drug's normal pharmacological action
Simple non-immune mechanical irritation of tissue
Complete absence of drug metabolism in all affected individuals
questions.correct_answer: Formation of a reactive drug metabolite that binds host proteins to create a neoantigen, triggering an immune-mediated hypersensitivity response
questions.explanation: Many idiosyncratic drug reactions arise when a reactive metabolite (often generated by CYP450 bioactivation) haptenates a host protein, and the immune system recognizes the resulting adduct as foreign, mounting a hypersensitivity response that is unpredictable and not simply dose-dependent.

questions.question: Teratogenic risk from xenobiotic exposure during pregnancy is generally understood to be highest during which period of gestation?
options: The period of organogenesis (roughly weeks 3-8), when developing organ systems are most sensitive to structural disruption
The final trimester, when the fetus is largest
Only in the first two weeks post-conception, the pre-implantation period
Teratogenic risk is constant and identical throughout all of gestation
questions.correct_answer: The period of organogenesis (roughly weeks 3-8), when developing organ systems are most sensitive to structural disruption
questions.explanation: Organogenesis is the critical window when rapidly differentiating tissues are most vulnerable to teratogenic insult, so exposure during this period carries the highest risk of major structural malformations, whereas exposure before implantation tends to follow an 'all-or-nothing' pattern and later exposure more often affects growth and functional maturation.

questions.question: Plasma protein binding of a drug (e.g. to albumin) primarily influences pharmacokinetics in which way?
options: Only the free (unbound) fraction of drug is pharmacologically active and available for distribution, metabolism, and excretion
Protein-bound drug is the only form capable of crossing cell membranes to reach its target
Protein binding has no influence on a drug's volume of distribution or clearance
Protein-bound drug is metabolized faster than free drug
questions.correct_answer: Only the free (unbound) fraction of drug is pharmacologically active and available for distribution, metabolism, and excretion
questions.explanation: Only unbound drug can cross membranes to reach receptors, be filtered by the glomerulus, or be accessible to metabolizing enzymes; highly protein-bound drugs act as a circulating reservoir, and displacement interactions can transiently raise the free, active fraction.

questions.question: Clearance (CL) in pharmacokinetics is best defined as:
options: The volume of plasma from which a drug is completely removed per unit time
The total amount of drug remaining in the body at steady state
The time required for plasma concentration to fall by half
The fraction of an oral dose that reaches systemic circulation
questions.correct_answer: The volume of plasma from which a drug is completely removed per unit time
questions.explanation: Clearance expresses the efficiency of drug elimination as an equivalent volume of plasma fully cleared of drug per unit time, and is the key parameter used to calculate maintenance dosing rate at steady state.

questions.question: Half-life (t1/2) and clearance (CL) are related to volume of distribution (Vd) by which approximate relationship?
options: t1/2 is directly proportional to Vd and inversely proportional to CL (t1/2 ≈ 0.693 x Vd / CL)
t1/2 is independent of both Vd and CL
t1/2 is inversely proportional to Vd and directly proportional to CL
CL is directly proportional to t1/2 with no relation to Vd
questions.correct_answer: t1/2 is directly proportional to Vd and inversely proportional to CL (t1/2 ≈ 0.693 x Vd / CL)
questions.explanation: Because t1/2 = 0.693 x Vd / CL, a drug with a large volume of distribution or low clearance will have a longer half-life, which is important for predicting dosing intervals and time to steady state.

questions.question: Enterohepatic circulation of a drug conjugate (e.g. a glucuronide) can prolong a drug's duration of action through which mechanism?
options: Gut bacterial beta-glucuronidase hydrolyzes the conjugate back to free drug in the intestine, allowing reabsorption into the portal circulation
The conjugate is permanently trapped in bile and never re-enters circulation
The conjugate is directly reabsorbed as-is by active transport in the stomach
Enterohepatic circulation only affects drugs given intravenously
questions.correct_answer: Gut bacterial beta-glucuronidase hydrolyzes the conjugate back to free drug in the intestine, allowing reabsorption into the portal circulation
questions.explanation: Biliary-excreted glucuronide conjugates can be deconjugated by intestinal bacterial beta-glucuronidases, regenerating the active parent drug, which is then reabsorbed and recirculated, effectively prolonging the drug's systemic exposure.

questions.question: Methylation as a Phase II reaction, using S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor, is a particularly important detoxification/metabolic route for which class of endogenous and exogenous compounds?
options: Catecholamines and other compounds bearing hydroxyl or amine groups (e.g. via catechol-O-methyltransferase)
Long-chain fatty acids exclusively
Glucuronic acid molecules
Heavy metal cations exclusively
questions.correct_answer: Catecholamines and other compounds bearing hydroxyl or amine groups (e.g. via catechol-O-methyltransferase)
questions.explanation: Methyltransferases such as catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) use SAM to methylate hydroxyl or amine groups on substrates like catecholamines and certain xenobiotics, altering their activity and aiding elimination.

questions.question: ED50 in pharmacodynamics refers to:
options: The dose that produces a specified therapeutic effect in 50% of a test population
The dose that is lethal in 50% of a test population
The dose at which 50% of a drug is eliminated from the body
The concentration at which a drug is 50% bound to plasma protein
questions.correct_answer: The dose that produces a specified therapeutic effect in 50% of a test population
questions.explanation: ED50 (median effective dose) is the dose required to produce a defined effect in half of the subjects tested, and is used together with TD50/LD50 to calculate the therapeutic index.
